hints: Think about what pH is measuring on a log scale and which ion concentration controls acidity.
For a weak acid dissociation $\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-$, recall how any equilibrium constant is written as products over reactants.
walkthrough:
Link pH to hydrogen ion concentration**
You know strong acids feel very different from very dilute acids because $[\text{H}^+]$ can vary by powers of ten. To compress that huge range we use a log scale. pH is simply the negative base 10 log of the hydrogen ion concentration, so $\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$.

Write Ka like any equilibrium constant**
Picture the weak acid partly dissociating: $\text{HA(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+\text{(aq)} + \text{A}^-\text{(aq)}$. Like all $K_c$ expressions, put concentrations of products on top and undissociated acid below. That gives $K_a = [\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]/[\text{HA}]$ with units of $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.

hints: Identify the large reservoir species in the mixture: which one can mop up added $\text{H}^+$ and which one can mop up added $\text{OH}^-$.
Write each removal as a simple neutralisation to reform the weak acid or its conjugate base, keeping the ratio almost unchanged.
walkthrough:
See what the buffer contains in large amounts**
You have a weak acid $\text{HA}$ sitting together with lots of its conjugate base $\text{A}^-$ from fully ionised $\text{NaA}$. That means you have a ready supply of base to deal with extra acid, and a ready supply of acid to deal with extra alkali. The $[\text{HA}]/[\text{A}^-]$ ratio therefore barely shifts.

Remove added H+ using conjugate base**
When $\text{H}^+$ is added, the $\text{A}^-$ ions act as a sink: $\text{A}^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{HA}$. The strong acid is converted into little dissociated weak acid, so $[\text{H}^+]$ stays almost constant.

Remove added OH- using weak acid**
When $\text{OH}^-$ is added, the undissociated $\text{HA}$ neutralises it: $\text{HA} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{A}^-$. The strong alkali is removed and replaced by $\text{A}^-$, again keeping pH almost unchanged.

Final answer: added acid: $\text{A}^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{HA}$
added alkali: $\text{HA} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{A}^-$

hints: Work out moles first: $\text{NaOH}$ neutralises the strong acid $\text{HCl}$ completely before it touches the weak acid $\text{HClO}$, so find how much $\text{NaOH}$ is left over.
Use the leftover $\text{OH}^-$ to find moles of $\text{HClO}$ remaining and moles of $\text{ClO}^-$ formed by $\text{HClO} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{ClO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Apply $K_a = [\text{H}^+][\text{ClO}^-]/[\text{HClO}]$ rearranged for $[\text{H}^+]$, or $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log([\text{salt}]/[\text{acid}])$, remembering volume is $1.00 \text{ dm}^3$ so moles equal concentration.
walkthrough:
Sort out which acid reacts first**
You start with $0.170 \text{ mol}$ of strong acid $\text{HCl}$ plus $0.170 \text{ mol}$ of weak acid $\text{HClO}$ in $1.00 \text{ dm}^3$. Added $\text{OH}^-$ will wipe out the strong acid first because that reaction goes to completion. So $0.170 \text{ mol}$ of your $0.200 \text{ mol}$ $\text{NaOH}$ is used up on $\text{HCl}$, leaving: $$n(\text{OH}^- \text{ left}) = 0.200 - 0.170 = 0.030 \text{ mol}$$

Build the buffer amounts**
That remaining $0.030 \text{ mol}$ $\text{OH}^-$ now partially neutralises the weak acid: $$\text{HClO} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{ClO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ So acid consumed $= 0.030 \text{ mol}$ and salt formed $= 0.030 \text{ mol}$. That leaves: $$n(\text{HClO}) = 0.170 - 0.030 = 0.140 \text{ mol}$$ $$n(\text{ClO}^-) = 0.030 \text{ mol}$$ Because the total volume is $1.00 \text{ dm}^3$, these mole values are numerically equal to concentrations in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.

Calculate [H+] then pH**
Now you have a classic acidic buffer. Rearrange the $K_a$ expression: $$[\text{H}^+] = K_a \times \dfrac{[\text{HA}]}{[\text{A}^-]} = 2.9 \times 10^{-8} \times \dfrac{0.14}{0.03}$$ $$[\text{H}^+] = 1.35 \times 10^{-7} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ Finally: $$\text{pH} = -\log(1.35 \times 10^{-7}) = 6.87$$ This makes sense, slightly acidic and close to $\text{p}K_a$ of $7.54$, as expected for water purification near pH 7.

Final answer: Volume $= 1000 \text{ cm}^3 = 1.00 \text{ dm}^3$, so $[\text{HClO}]_{initial} = 0.170 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ and $[\text{HCl}]_{initial} = 0.170 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.
$n(\text{NaOH})$ left after $\text{HCl}$ neutralisation $= 0.200 - 0.170 = 0.030 \text{ mol}$.
Remaining $n(\text{HClO}) = 0.170 - 0.030 = 0.140 \text{ mol}$, $n(\text{ClO}^-) = 0.030 \text{ mol}$.
$[\text{H}^+] = K_a \times \dfrac{[\text{HClO}]}{[\text{ClO}^-]} = 2.9 \times 10^{-8} \times \dfrac{0.14}{0.03} = 1.35 \times 10^{-7} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
$\text{pH} = -\log(1.35 \times 10^{-7}) = 6.87$
